name: Oskar Morgenstern
milestone_by_age_26: PhD at 23 and professorship at Vienna at 26 were standard academic steps; his seminal work Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (with von Neumann) was published in 1944 at age 42. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Morgenstern grew up in Vienna, earned his PhD in political science from the University of Vienna in 1925 at age 23, then undertook a Rockefeller Foundation fellowship before returning as a professor in 1928. His collaboration with von Neumann that produced game theory began in 1939 at Princeton.
family_context_summary: Son of merchant Wilhelm Morgenstern and Margarete Teichler; grew up in a middle-class household in Vienna after moving from Görlitz at age 12.
evidence_summary: Morgenstern earned his PhD at 23 and became a professor at 26, but these were standard academic milestones. His foundational contribution to game theory came at 42 with the 1944 publication of Theory of Games and Economic Behavior with John von Neumann.

name: Lloyd Shapley
milestone_by_age_26: Was a Harvard undergraduate and then starting at RAND by age 26; his PhD (1953) and seminal Shapley value work came at age 30. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Shapley grew up in Cambridge, MA as the son of astronomer Harlow Shapley, attended Phillips Exeter Academy and Harvard, but was drafted into the Army Air Corps in 1943 where he earned a Bronze Star for breaking a Soviet weather code. After the war he worked briefly at RAND before pursuing his PhD at Princeton, completed in 1953.
family_context_summary: Born to renowned Harvard astronomer Harlow Shapley and Martha Betz Shapley; grew up in the director's residence at the Harvard Observatory in a scientifically immersed family.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Harlow Shapley was a prominent astronomer who directed the Harvard Observatory, providing an elite scientific environment from childhood.
evidence_summary: Despite an elite scientific family background and Bronze Star service, Shapley had no material milestone by 26. His PhD and the Shapley value came at 30, and the Gale-Shapley algorithm at 39. The Nobel Prize followed in 2012.

name: Alvin Roth
milestone_by_age_26: PhD from Stanford at 23 and faculty position at UIUC by 26 were standard academic steps; his seminal market design contributions and Nobel Prize came decades later. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Roth grew up in Queens, NY, the son of public high school teachers. He entered Columbia's engineering school at 16, earned his BS, then completed a PhD in operations research at Stanford in 1974 at age 23. He took a position at the University of Illinois and later moved to Pittsburgh and Harvard.
family_context_summary: Born in Queens to Ernest and Lillian Roth, both public high school teachers of Secretarial Studies; a middle-class Jewish family with strong educational emphasis.
evidence_summary: Roth earned his PhD at 23 from Stanford and was a faculty member by 26, but these were standard academic milestones. His transformative work on market design, matching algorithms, and kidney exchange came in the 1980s-2000s, earning the Nobel Prize in 2012.

name: David Gale
milestone_by_age_26: Had only completed an MA by 26; his PhD (1949) and the Gale-Shapley algorithm (1962) came later. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Gale grew up in and around New York City, earned a BA from Swarthmore in 1943, an MA from the University of Michigan in 1947, and a PhD from Princeton in 1949 under Albert Tucker. His most famous work, the Gale-Shapley deferred acceptance algorithm, was published in 1962.
family_context_summary: Born in Manhattan; family background not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Gale had only an MA by age 26. His PhD from Princeton came at 28, and his most influential contributions—the Gale-Shapley algorithm and his work on linear programming—came in the 1950s and 1960s.

name: Herbert Simon
milestone_by_age_26: Had a BA and a co-authored municipal administration book by 22, but his PhD came at 27 (1943) and his seminal bounded rationality and AI work came in the 1950s. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Simon entered the University of Chicago at 17, earned his BA in 1936, co-authored a book on measuring municipal activities in 1938, and worked as a research assistant while pursuing his doctorate, which he completed in 1943 at age 27. His groundbreaking work on bounded rationality and AI came after joining Carnegie Tech in 1949.
family_context_summary: Born in Milwaukee to an electrical engineer father (who emigrated from Germany) and an accomplished pianist mother; middle-class family with European immigrant roots.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an electrical engineer and patent attorney; not a direct domain transfer to economics or AI but provided a technical/professional household environment.
evidence_summary: Simon had a BA and a co-authored book by 22, but his PhD came at 27 and his seminal contributions—bounded rationality, AI with Newell, the Turing Award (1975), and Nobel Prize (1978)—all came well after age 26.

name: Allen Newell
milestone_by_age_26: Was a research scientist at RAND by 26 but had not yet produced his pioneering work; the Logic Theorist (1956) came at 29 and the General Problem Solver at 30. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Newell earned his BS in physics from Stanford in 1949, spent a year at Princeton, then joined the RAND Corporation in 1950 where he was exposed to game theory and early computing. His pioneering AI work with Herbert Simon began in the mid-1950s, producing the Logic Theorist in 1956.
family_context_summary: Born in San Francisco to Robert R. Newell, a prominent professor of radiology at Stanford Medical School, and Jeanette La Valley Newell; grew up in an academic/professional household.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a prominent Stanford Medical School professor; not a direct domain transfer to AI but provided an elite academic environment and research-oriented role model.
evidence_summary: Newell was at RAND by 26 but had not yet produced his pioneering AI work. The Logic Theorist (1956, age 29), General Problem Solver (1957), and Turing Award (1975) all came well after age 26.

name: Edward Feigenbaum
milestone_by_age_26: Developed EPAM (Elementary Perceiver and Memorizer), one of the first computer models of human learning, as his PhD thesis at Carnegie Tech under Herbert Simon, completed in 1960 at age 24.
early_history_summary: Feigenbaum started college at 16, earned his BS from Carnegie Tech in 1956 and his PhD in 1960 under Herbert Simon, supported by a Ford Foundation Fellowship. His thesis work on EPAM was a pioneering contribution to computational cognitive science, simulating human verbal learning behavior on a computer.
family_context_summary: Born to a culturally Jewish family in Weehawken, New Jersey; moved to North Bergen and attended public schools. Family financial background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Carnegie Tech, Herbert Simon mentorship, early AI access, Ford Foundation fellowship, early college entry
evidence_summary: Feigenbaum entered college at 16 and completed his PhD by 24 at Carnegie Tech under Herbert Simon, one of the founding figures of AI. His thesis produced EPAM, one of the first computer models of human learning, a pioneering contribution to both AI and cognitive psychology. The Carnegie Tech environment with Simon and Newell was one of the world's premier early AI research centers. He was supported by a Ford Foundation Fellowship. Family background is not well documented beyond being a culturally Jewish family in New Jersey.
starting_point: Born to a culturally Jewish family in Weehawken, New Jersey; moved to nearby North Bergen and attended public schools before starting college at age 16. Family occupation and financial status not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Kumagai Professor of Computer Science Emeritus at Stanford University; widely known as the 'father of expert systems'; Turing Award winner (1994).

trajectory.event: Completed BS at Carnegie Institute of Technology (now Carnegie Mellon University).
Completed PhD at Carnegie Tech under Herbert Simon, developing EPAM, one of the first computer models of human learning.
Joined Stanford University faculty and co-founded the DENDRAL project with Joshua Lederberg, creating the world's first expert system.
Won the ACM Turing Award jointly with Raj Reddy for pioneering large-scale AI systems.
Serves as Kumagai Professor of Computer Science Emeritus at Stanford University.

name: Terry Winograd
milestone_by_age_26: Created SHRDLU, a groundbreaking natural language understanding program, as his PhD thesis at the MIT AI Lab, completed in 1970 at age 24.
early_history_summary: Winograd grew up in Colorado, earned his BA in mathematics from Colorado College in 1966, spent a year studying linguistics at University College London, then pursued his PhD at MIT under Seymour Papert. He developed SHRDLU from 1968 to 1970, a program that could understand and respond to natural language commands about a blocks world.
family_context_summary: Born in Takoma Park, Maryland; grew up in Colorado. Family background and parental occupations not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: MIT AI Lab, Seymour Papert advisor, PDP-6 computer access, frontier NLP research, blocks world
evidence_summary: Winograd developed SHRDLU at the MIT AI Lab from 1968-1970 under Seymour Papert, creating one of the most influential early natural language understanding programs. The MIT AI Lab provided access to a PDP-6 computer and a community of leading AI researchers, making it arguably the premier AI research environment in the world at that time. His background in both mathematics (Colorado College) and linguistics (UCL) gave him an interdisciplinary foundation. Family background is not documented in reviewed sources.
starting_point: Born in Takoma Park, Maryland; grew up in Colorado and graduated from Colorado College. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Professor Emeritus of Computer Science at Stanford University; known for SHRDLU and HCI research; received ACM SIGCHI Lifetime Research Achievement Award in 2011; advised Google founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin.

trajectory.event: Graduated with a BA in mathematics from Colorado College.
Studied linguistics at University College London, building interdisciplinary foundation for NLP work.
Completed SHRDLU at the MIT AI Lab, a groundbreaking natural language understanding program that became his PhD thesis.
Joined the Stanford University faculty in the Computer Science Department.
Published 'Understanding Computers and Cognition' with Fernando Flores, marking a major philosophical departure in AI thinking.
Received the ACM SIGCHI Lifetime Research Achievement Award for contributions to human-computer interaction.

name: Roger Schank
milestone_by_age_26: Pioneered conceptual dependency theory in natural language understanding, completing his PhD at the University of Texas at Austin in 1969 at age 23 and presenting at COLING 1969.
early_history_summary: Schank attended Stuyvesant High School in Manhattan, studied mathematics at Carnegie Mellon for his undergraduate degree, then completed a PhD in linguistics at the University of Texas at Austin in 1969. His thesis introduced conceptual dependency theory, a framework for representing meaning in natural language that became influential in early NLP and AI research. He joined Stanford as an assistant professor in 1968.
family_context_summary: Born in Manhattan, New York; attended Stuyvesant High School, a prestigious specialized exam-admission public school. Family occupation and financial background not documented in reviewed sources.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Stuyvesant High School, Carnegie Mellon undergraduate, Stanford AI Lab, early NLP theory, COLING 1969
evidence_summary: Schank attended Stuyvesant High School and studied mathematics at Carnegie Mellon before completing a PhD in linguistics at UT Austin at 23, pioneering conceptual dependency theory for NLP. He was associated with the Stanford AI Lab (his thesis was also issued as Stanford AI Memo 83) and presented his parser at COLING 1969. The interdisciplinary combination of mathematics, linguistics, and computing positioned him at the frontier of early NLP. Family background beyond attending Stuyvesant is not documented.
starting_point: Born in Manhattan, New York; attended Stuyvesant High School, a prestigious exam-admission public school. Family occupation and financial background not documented in reviewed sources.
current_position: Died January 29, 2023, at age 76 in Shelburne, Vermont; final roles were Chairman and CEO of Socratic Arts and founder of Engines for Education.

trajectory.event: Joined Stanford University as assistant professor, affiliated with the Stanford AI Lab.
Completed PhD at UT Austin pioneering conceptual dependency theory and presented a conceptual dependency parser at COLING 1969.
Became professor of computer science and psychology at Yale University.
Co-founded the academic journal Cognitive Science, helping establish cognitive science as a discipline.
Founded the Institute for the Learning Sciences at Northwestern University with $30M from Andersen Consulting.
Died on January 29, 2023, in Shelburne, Vermont.

name: Raj Reddy
milestone_by_age_26: Was working as an IBM Applied Science Representative in Australia by 26; his PhD (1966) and pioneering speech recognition systems (Hearsay I, 1970s) came later. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Reddy grew up in Katur village in Andhra Pradesh, India, the first in his family to attend college. He earned a BE in civil engineering from the University of Madras in 1958, an MTech from the University of New South Wales in 1960, then worked at IBM in Australia before pursuing a PhD at Stanford, completed in 1966. His pioneering work on continuous speech recognition came in the 1970s at Carnegie Mellon.
family_context_summary: Born in Katur village, Andhra Pradesh, India; father was a landowner, mother a homemaker; first in family to attend college. Rural upbringing with limited educational infrastructure.
evidence_summary: Reddy was working at IBM in Australia by 26, having completed engineering degrees in India and Australia. His PhD from Stanford came at 29, and his pioneering speech recognition systems (Hearsay I, Hearsay II) were developed in the 1970s at CMU. The Turing Award came in 1994.

name: Frederick Jelinek
milestone_by_age_26: Was a graduate student at MIT by 26; his PhD (c. 1962) and pioneering statistical speech recognition work at IBM came in the 1970s. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Jelinek was born in Czechoslovakia; his father died in the Terezin concentration camp during the Nazi occupation. His mother emigrated with him to New York, where he attended City College before transferring to MIT. He graduated from MIT around 1956 and began his doctorate in information theory under Robert Fano, later teaching at Cornell for a decade before joining IBM Research in the early 1970s where he pioneered statistical approaches to speech recognition.
family_context_summary: Born in Kladno, Czechoslovakia to a Jewish dentist father who died in the Terezin concentration camp and a Swiss-born mother who converted to Judaism; emigrated to New York after WWII. Significant childhood adversity from Nazi occupation and loss of father.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a dentist; not a direct domain transfer to information theory or speech recognition.
evidence_summary: Jelinek was a graduate student at MIT by 26, having survived the Nazi occupation of Czechoslovakia and emigrated to the US. His PhD came around 1962 at age 30, and his pioneering statistical methods for speech recognition were developed at IBM in the 1970s-1990s.

name: Lawrence Rabiner
milestone_by_age_26: Had a PhD from MIT (1967, age 24) and was a research staff member at Bell Labs by 26, but his influential textbooks and major DSP publications came in the 1970s. No material milestone by 26.
early_history_summary: Rabiner grew up in Brooklyn, earned SB and SM degrees simultaneously from MIT in 1964 and a PhD in 1967, all in electrical engineering. He joined Bell Labs' research division in 1967 through connections made during a cooperative program. His influential textbooks on digital signal processing and speech processing were published starting in 1975.
family_context_summary: Born in Brooklyn, New York. Family background not documented in reviewed sources.
evidence_summary: Rabiner had a PhD from MIT at 24 and joined Bell Labs, but his influential contributions—the textbooks on digital signal processing (1975) and speech processing (1978)—came well after age 26. His career at Bell Labs spanned from 1967 to 2002, with major publications in the 1970s-1990s.
